concept.name: Ascending triangle
concept.definition: A classical consolidation pattern bounded above by a horizontal resistance line drawn through two or more comparable highs and below by a rising trend line drawn through successively higher lows. It carries a bullish bias — interpreted as accumulation against a fixed supply level — and usually resolves as a continuation of the prior uptrend, though it occasionally forms as a bottom reversal. It is a technical-analysis hypothesis, not a proven predictive law.
concept.intuition: Sellers defend a fixed ceiling while buyers keep stepping in at higher and higher prices; the rising floor shows buying pressure building until the ceiling finally gives way.
concept.mechanics: Require at least two reaction highs at similar levels for the horizontal line and at least two successively higher reaction lows for the ascending line (a new low equal to or below the prior low invalidates the pattern). Volume typically contracts during formation and should expand on the upside breakout; broken resistance often turns into support on a return move. The target projects the pattern's widest height up from the breakout.
concept.formula: Price target = B + (H - L), where B = breakout (horizontal resistance) price, and H - L = the widest vertical distance of the triangle.
concept.failure_modes: Breakouts can fail or reverse ('busted' patterns), especially when volume does not expand or when the pattern forms very late in a mature uptrend. A downside break of the rising trend line converts the 'bullish' pattern into a failure and often a fast decline.
concept.misconceptions: That the bullish bias justifies buying inside the pattern before the breakout — the bias is only a tendency, and the pattern is not actionable until resistance actually breaks.
concept.example: A stock bumps against $24 three times over five months while its lows rise from $14 to $20; it then breaks $24 on heavy volume, projecting a measured move toward $34.
